person.name: Friedensreich_Hundertwasser
person.summary: Friedensreich Hundertwasser (born Friedrich Stowasser) was an Austrian artist, architectural designer, and environmentalist known for his colorful, organic paintings and his radical, anti-rectilinear approach to architecture. After early travels and exposure to avant‑garde art in postwar Europe, he developed a personal style that rejected straight lines and standardized forms, advocating instead for individuality, nature‑integrated buildings, and ecological living. From the 1970s onward he realized numerous building projects in Europe and beyond, promoted green roofs and "tree tenants," and lived a peripatetic life between Austria and New Zealand until his death at sea in 2000.

chapters.headline: Childhood, War, and First Art
chapters.description: An only child in interwar Vienna, Friedrich Stowasser grew up amid family loss, Nazi persecution, and early recognition of his artistic talent, experiences that shaped his lifelong individualism and attachment to nature.

chapters.headline: Travels and Artistic Breakthrough
chapters.description: As a young man he briefly attended art academy, adopted the name Hundertwasser, and roamed Europe and North Africa, absorbing influences and formulating his own theory of painting and perception while gaining international recognition.

chapters.headline: Retreats, Nature, and Global Reach
chapters.description: Increasingly successful, Hundertwasser withdrew to rural retreats while expanding his exhibitions worldwide, deepening his ecological thinking, and laying the foundations for his later architectural and environmental projects.

chapters.headline: Architecture and Ecological Activism
chapters.description: In his later decades he became a celebrated architectural designer and public environmental advocate, realized landmark buildings, engaged in high‑profile protests, and divided his life between Europe and his reforestation project in New Zealand until his death.

events.title: Birth in Vienna
events.description: Friedrich Stowasser, later known as Friedensreich Hundertwasser, was born in Vienna as the only child of engineer Ernst Stowasser and Elsa Stowasser, née Scheuer, who was of Jewish origin. His family background combined roots in Bohemia on his father’s side and Moravia on his mother’s side, foreshadowing his later sense of Central European identity.

events.date_note: Father died when he was about one year old
events.title: Early death of his father
events.description: Around his first birthday, Hundertwasser’s father Ernst died suddenly of appendicitis, leaving Elsa to raise their son alone in Vienna. Growing up fatherless during a turbulent period contributed to his sensitivity and independence, traits that would later be reflected in his rejection of conventional paths in art and life.

events.title: Montessori school and baptism
events.description: At about six to seven years old, Hundertwasser attended a Montessori school in Vienna, where art teachers praised his exceptional sense for form and color. In the same year he was baptized Catholic, a step that likely offered some protection in a society increasingly hostile to Jews and that later fed into his complex relationship with religion and identity.

images.caption: Exhibition of paintings and graphic works by Friedensreich Hundertwasser from the Würth Collection, illustrating the kind of color- and form-rich art for which he had shown talent since childhood.

events.date_note: Year of the Anschluss of Austria to Nazi Germany
events.title: Nazi persecution and forced relocation
events.description: After [[Anschluss|Nazi Germany annexed Austria]], Hundertwasser’s life as a child of a Jewish mother changed drastically: he was placed in the [[Hitler Youth|Hitler Youth]] while his mother tried to shield him by moving him from a private to a state school. Mother and son were forcibly resettled with other Jews into a crowded house in Vienna’s [[Leopoldstadt|Leopoldstadt district]], where they survived the war while his maternal grandmother and some 70 relatives were deported and murdered.

Anschluss.explanation: The "Anschluss" was the annexation of Austria into Nazi Germany in March 1938, which brought Austrian Jews under Nazi racial laws and persecution.

Hitler Youth.explanation: The Hitler Youth was the youth organization of the Nazi Party, which aimed to indoctrinate boys and girls with Nazi ideology and prepare them for service to the regime.

Leopoldstadt.explanation: Leopoldstadt is Vienna’s 2nd district, which before and during World War II had a large Jewish population and was a focal area for persecution and forced housing of Jews under Nazi rule.

events.title: Matura and brief art academy studies
events.description: In 1948 Hundertwasser completed his secondary education with the [[Matura|Matura]] at the [[Bundesgymnasium Horn|Bundesgymnasium]] in Horn. That autumn he enrolled at the [[Academy of Fine Arts Vienna|Academy of Fine Arts]] in Vienna, but he stayed only about three months before abandoning formal study, dissatisfied with academic norms and already convinced he had to find his own path as an artist.

Matura.explanation: The Matura is the school-leaving examination in Austria and some other European countries, qualifying students for university entrance.

Bundesgymnasium Horn.explanation: Bundesgymnasium Horn is a federal academic secondary school (Gymnasium) in the town of Horn, Lower Austria.

Academy of Fine Arts Vienna.explanation: The Academy of Fine Arts Vienna is a renowned Austrian art school, founded in 1692, offering higher education in the visual arts and architecture.

events.title: First Italian journey and name "Hundertwasser"
events.description: In April 1949 he traveled for the first time to Italy, beginning a pattern of restless artistic wandering. During this period he began signing his works with the artist name Hundertwasser, a Germanized play on his birth name Stowasser (with "[[sto|sto]]" meaning "hundred" in several Slavic languages), marking a conscious reinvention of his identity as an artist.

images.caption: Textile design by Friedensreich Hundertwasser, reflecting the distinctive visual style he developed after his postwar travels and artistic self-reinvention.

sto.explanation: In several Slavic languages (such as Czech and Slovak), the word or root "sto" means "one hundred," which Hundertwasser used as the basis for Germanizing his birth name Stowasser into Hundertwasser.

events.date_note: Travel period in the first half of 1951
events.title: Formative travels in North Africa
events.description: In the early 1950s Hundertwasser undertook extensive journeys to Morocco, Tunisia, and later Sicily, immersing himself in North African light, color, and [[vernacular architecture|vernacular architecture]]. He later described the impressions from this trip as decisive for his painting, reinforcing his fascination with vibrant, organic forms and the [[ensouled nature|"ensouled nature"]] that would dominate his imagery.

images.caption: The Waldspirale residential complex in Darmstadt, Germany, designed by Friedensreich Hundertwasser, illustrating the vibrant colors and organic forms that his earlier travels helped to shape.

vernacular architecture.explanation: Architecture designed based on local needs, materials, and traditions, typically without formal architectural training and reflecting a region’s cultural and environmental conditions.

ensouled nature.explanation: A key notion in Hundertwasser’s aesthetic and ecological thinking, referring to nature as a living, spiritually animated presence rather than inert matter.

events.date_note: Span of his first important solo exhibitions in Europe
events.title: First major exhibitions in Europe
events.description: Between 1952 and 1956 Hundertwasser’s paintings were shown in solo exhibitions in Vienna, Milan, and the Galerie Facchetti in Paris, bringing him to the attention of the postwar European avant‑garde. Living mainly in Paris at the time, he engaged with debates between geometric and expressive abstraction and began formulating his own approach, which rejected the straight line and emphasized spirals, vivid colors, and individual perception.

images.caption: Ceramic mural panels by Friedensreich Hundertwasser in the Oriente metro station in Lisbon, illustrating his characteristic use of spirals, vivid colors, and irregular lines similar to the pictorial style he developed in the 1950s.

events.title: Buys Normandy farm and marries Herta Leitner
events.description: In 1957 Hundertwasser purchased a small farm on the edge of Normandy, securing a rural refuge from city life where he could live closer to nature. The following year he married the 16‑year‑old Herta Leitner in Gibraltar, entering briefly into conventional domesticity, though the marriage would end in divorce in 1960 as his itinerant, bohemian lifestyle proved incompatible with stable family life.

events.title: Guest professorship and "Unendliche Linie" action
events.description: In 1959 he became a guest lecturer at the Hochschule für bildende Künste in [[Hamburg|Hamburg]], where in December he staged the "[[Unendliche Linie|Unendliche Linie (Endless Line)]]" action with Bazon Brock, Herbert Schuldt, and students, drawing a continuous line through his classroom until the director halted the performance. When ordered to stop, Hundertwasser resigned his post, underscoring his principled opposition to institutional constraints and the "straight line" in art and life.

images.caption: The Waldspirale residential complex in Darmstadt, Germany, designed by Friedensreich Hundertwasser, illustrating his rejection of the straight line in architecture that underpinned actions such as the 1959 "Unendliche Linie" performance.

Hamburg.explanation: Hamburg is a city-state in northern West Germany where the Hochschule für bildende Künste (University of Fine Arts) served as an important postwar centre for experimental art and teaching.

Unendliche Linie.explanation: "Unendliche Linie" ("Endless Line") was a 1959 classroom action by Hundertwasser and collaborators in which a single continuous line was drawn through the teaching space as a performative critique of academic authority and the straight line in art.

events.title: First Japan visit and Mainichi Prize
events.description: In 1961 Hundertwasser traveled to [[Japan|Japan]], a country whose culture and aesthetics fascinated him, and participated in the [[Mainichi Art Exhibition|6th International Art Exhibition in Tokyo]]. There he received the prestigious Mainichi Prize, and during his stays in Japan over the following years he experimented with Japanese scripts to reshape his given name, a process that would culminate in his adopting the forename Friedensreich later in the decade.

images.caption: The Waldspirale residential complex in Darmstadt, Germany, designed by Friedensreich Hundertwasser, illustrating his mature architectural style that grew out of ideas he was already developing during his travels in the 1960s, including his visits to Japan.

Japan.explanation: Post‑war Japan became a major center for avant‑garde and international art exchanges, attracting many Western artists inspired by its aesthetics and traditions.

Mainichi Art Exhibition.explanation: An annual art exhibition in Japan organized by the Mainichi Newspapers company, associated with the conferral of the Mainichi Art Award (Mainichi Prize) on selected artists.

events.title: Venice Biennale retrospective breakthrough
events.description: In 1962 Hundertwasser achieved a major international breakthrough when the Austrian Pavilion at the [[Venice Biennale|Venice Biennale]] devoted a retrospective to his work, curated by Vinzenz Oberhammer. The show, followed by a traveling retrospective organized by the [[Kestner-Gesellschaft|Kestner‑Gesellschaft]] in Hannover and the publication of his first [[catalogue raisonné|catalogue raisonné]] by Wieland Schmied, established him as a prominent figure in postwar European art.

images.caption: The Waldspirale residential complex in Darmstadt, Germany, a later architectural work by Friedensreich Hundertwasser, illustrating the distinctive organic forms and colorful aesthetic that contributed to his international reputation established after the 1962 Venice Biennale retrospective.

Venice Biennale.explanation: A major international contemporary art exhibition held biennially in Venice that serves as one of the most prestigious platforms for artists worldwide.

Kestner-Gesellschaft.explanation: A contemporary art society and exhibition venue in Hanover, Germany, known for organizing influential modern and postwar art retrospectives.

catalogue raisonn\u00e9.explanation: A comprehensive, scholarly reference work that systematically lists and documents all known artworks by a particular artist.

events.title: Buys "Hahnsäge" retreat in Waldviertel
events.description: In 1966 Hundertwasser bought the disused "Hahnsäge" sawmill in the sparsely populated [[Waldviertel|Waldviertel region]] of Lower Austria and converted it into a rustic home and studio. Surrounded by forests and far from urban pressures, this base allowed him to live out his ideals of simplicity, closeness to nature, and self‑sufficiency while continuing to produce paintings and graphic works.

images.caption: Friedensreich Hundertwasser on rural land in New Zealand in 1998, reflecting his preference for simple, nature‑oriented living similar to his earlier retreat at the Hahnsäge in the Waldviertel.

Waldviertel.explanation: The Waldviertel is a sparsely populated, forested highland region in the northwest of Lower Austria, known for its rural landscapes and traditional villages.

events.title: American touring exhibition and ship "Regentag"
events.description: In 1968 Hundertwasser traveled to [[California|California]] to work with art historian Herschel Chipp on a major museum exhibition that toured several U.S. cities from 1968 to 1969. The same year he sailed an old salt freighter from [[Sicily|Sicily]] to [[Venice|Venice]], later transforming it into his beloved ship "Regentag" (Rainy Day), a floating studio and symbol of his seafaring, nomadic existence.

California.explanation: A U.S. state on the west coast where Hundertwasser collaborated with art historian Herschel B. Chipp on a touring museum exhibition of his work in 1968.

Sicily.explanation: The largest island in the Mediterranean Sea and an autonomous region of Italy; Hundertwasser acquired an old freighter here in 1968 before sailing it to Venice and converting it into his ship Regentag.

Venice.explanation: A historic port city in northeastern Italy, built on a lagoon; in 1968 it was the destination where Hundertwasser brought the freighter that he later transformed into his studio-ship Regentag.

events.title: Founds Gruener Janura AG rights company
events.description: In 1972 Hundertwasser founded the Swiss company [[Gruener Janura AG|Gruener Janura AG]] (later [[Namida AG|Namida AG]]) to manage his copyrights and reproductions, a sign of his growing commercial success and need for professional administration of his oeuvre. The structure allowed him to control how his works were printed, catalogued, and disseminated while he focused on creation and travel.

images.caption: The Green Citadel of Magdeburg, a later architectural work by Friedensreich Hundertwasser, illustrating the kind of oeuvre whose rights were managed through his companies Gruener Janura AG and Namida AG.

Gruener Janura AG.explanation: A Swiss company founded by Friedensreich Hundertwasser in 1972 in St. Gallen to administer his copyrights, reproductions, and commercial rights to his artworks.

Namida AG.explanation: The later name of Gruener Janura AG, the Swiss rights-management company handling Friedensreich Hundertwasser’s artistic and commercial interests.

events.title: Establishes New Zealand reforestation estate
events.description: Following a traveling exhibition in New Zealand and Australia, Hundertwasser first visited New Zealand in 1973 and soon acquired several properties encompassing the entire Kaurinui Valley in the Bay of Islands. There he embarked on a long‑term ecological project, planting over 100,000 native trees, building ponds and natural wastewater treatment systems, and living in simple structures such as a converted farmhouse and bottle house, seeking to return the land to nature.

locations.name_modern: Bay of Islands, Northland, New Zealand

images.caption: Friedensreich Hundertwasser on his land in New Zealand in 1998, part of the reforestation estate he began developing in the 1970s.

events.title: Activism at Hainburger Au occupation
events.description: In 1984 Hundertwasser took part in the citizens’ occupation of the [[Hainburger Au|Hainburger Au wetlands]] east of Vienna to protest a planned power plant, camping with activists in freezing temperatures. At a press conference he dramatically tore up, on camera, the high Austrian State Prize he had been awarded, signaling his willingness to sacrifice official honors in defense of nature and grassroots democracy.

Hainburger Au.explanation: The Hainburger Au is a floodplain forest and wetland area along the Danube near Hainburg an der Donau in eastern Austria, which became a major symbol of the Austrian environmental movement after a mass occupation in 1984 stopped a proposed power plant.

events.title: Completion of Vienna Hundertwasserhaus
events.description: On 17 February 1986, the [[Hundertwasserhaus|Hundertwasserhaus social housing complex]] in Vienna, a municipal apartment building designed in collaboration with architect Josef Krawina, was officially handed over to its tenants. With its irregular façade, colorful tiles, planted terraces, and undulating floors, the building became an icon of his architectural philosophy—rejecting rigid modernism in favor of individuality and the integration of trees and greenery into human dwellings.

images.caption: The Waldspirale residential complex in Darmstadt, another example of Friedensreich Hundertwasser's later residential architecture integrating irregular forms and greenery, comparable in concept to the earlier Vienna Hundertwasserhaus.

Hundertwasserhaus.explanation: A municipal apartment building in Vienna completed in 1985–86, designed by artist Friedensreich Hundertwasser with architect Josef Krawina, known for its irregular forms, bright colors, and integration of vegetation into the architecture.

events.title: Opening of KunstHausWien Museum Hundertwasser
events.description: On 9 April 1991 the KunstHausWien Museum Hundertwasser opened in Vienna in a former factory he had redesigned, providing the only permanent museum devoted to his work. The institution displays his youth works, paintings, graphics, tapestries, applied art, and architectural projects, consolidating his status as a major cultural figure while embodying his ideals of a lively, nature‑embracing built environment.

images.caption: The Waldspirale residential complex in Darmstadt, Germany, a later architectural work by Friedensreich Hundertwasser that reflects the same organic, irregular design principles showcased in KunstHausWien Museum Hundertwasser.

events.title: Death at sea and burial in New Zealand
events.description: On 19 February 2000 Hundertwasser died of heart failure aboard the ocean liner [[Queen Elizabeth 2|Queen Elizabeth 2]] during a return voyage from [[New Zealand|New Zealand]] to Europe. In accordance with his wishes he was buried on his New Zealand property, without a coffin and wrapped in a shroud bearing his own [[koru‑flag|koru‑flag]] design, with a tulip tree planted above his grave—his final personal union of art, body, and living nature.

images.caption: Public toilets in Kawakawa, New Zealand, designed by Friedensreich Hundertwasser near the area where he lived and was buried.

Queen Elizabeth 2.explanation: A British ocean liner operated by the Cunard Line from 1969 to 2008, used primarily for transatlantic crossings and cruises.

New Zealand.explanation: An island country in the southwestern Pacific Ocean where Hundertwasser maintained a rural property and chose to be buried.

koru\u2011flag.explanation: A personal flag design by Hundertwasser based on the Māori koru spiral motif, symbolizing new life, growth, and harmony with nature.
